examples.label: CPTS Ch06 — scan example.com for weak TLS

notes: sslscan/testssl.sh enumerate supported TLS versions, ciphers, and cert details. Flag SSLv2/3, TLS1.0/1.1, weak ciphers (RC4/DES/EXPORT), Heartbleed, and expired/self-signed certs. Low-severity findings but common report content. sslscan reports: supported protocol versions (SSLv2/3, TLSv1.0-1.3), preferred ciphers per protocol, certificate details (expiry, CN, SAN). Red = weak/broken. Look for TLSv1.0/1.1 (deprecated), RC4/DES ciphers, self-signed or expired certs. Also covered in: CPTS Ch06 (Vulnerability Assessment).

recommended.note: Fingerprint the web stack behind the TLS.

name: sslscan - Check SSL/TLS Configuration
description: Enumerate a host's supported SSL/TLS protocols, ciphers, and certificate details to flag weak/expiring/revoked configurations.

defense.why_it_works: sslscan connects to a TLS-enabled service and enumerates the supported protocol versions, cipher suites, and certificate details to surface weak or deprecated configurations (SSLv2/3, weak ciphers, expired/self-signed certs, known flaws like Heartbleed).
defense.prerequisites: Network access to a TLS-enabled service (e.g. TCP 443).
defense.impact: A list of SSL/TLS weaknesses - deprecated protocols, weak ciphers, certificate issues - as report findings and possible downgrade/MITM avenues.
defense.detection: Low: a series of TLS handshake attempts with varying protocol/cipher parameters to one service. Visible in the server's TLS/connection logs but not strongly alerting. [MITRE T1595.002 AN1999] anomalous handshake patterns can be correlated in network monitoring.
defense.artifacts: Multiple TLS handshakes/negotiations from one source to the service in connection logs.
defense.prevention: Disable deprecated protocols (SSLv2/3, TLS 1.0/1.1) and weak ciphers, and keep certificates valid - this hardens against both the finding and real downgrade attacks. [MITRE T1595.002 M1056].
defense.evasion: Handshakes are few and low-noise; spacing them out keeps the footprint minimal.
defense.misconfiguration: Vulnerability scanning reveals services with unpatched CVEs, default configurations, or known-weak settings. The absence of a patch management process allows critical vulnerabilities to remain exploitable for months or years. Scan results that are not acted upon create a false sense of security.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# OpenVAS/Nessus finding typical vulnerable targets:
# CVSSv3: 9.8 - Apache Struts2 RCE (CVE-2017-5638) - unpatched
# CVSSv3: 8.8 - Tomcat manager with default creds (admin/admin)
# CVSSv3: 10.0 - MS17-010 (EternalBlue) - SMBv1 enabled, unpatched

# Unpatched = patch not applied within SLA:
# Critical (CVSS 9+): patch within 24-72 hours
# High (CVSS 7-8.9): patch within 7 days
# Medium: patch within 30 days
defense.secure_config:
# Establish a vulnerability management program:
# 1. Scan weekly with authenticated scans (Nessus/OpenVAS/Qualys)
# 2. Integrate scan results with ticketing (Jira/ServiceNow)
# 3. Set SLA by severity: Critical 72h, High 7d, Medium 30d
# 4. Verify patches with re-scan

# CVSS scoring -> risk-based prioritization:
# Not all CVSSv3 9+ are exploitable in your environment
# Use EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) to prioritize by actual exploitation likelihood

# Defense-in-depth: patch is the fix, but compensating controls while patching:
# WAF rule for web vuln CVEs
# Network segment to isolate vulnerable service
# IDS signature for exploit traffic
